resources.string: A row, column or box has exactly one empty cell. Find the digit missing from its eight filled cells.
Every region contains 1–9 exactly once, so its missing digit must occupy the only empty cell. For example, a row containing 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9 must end with 5.
Count empty cells in one region. This is the simplest single; it does not require pencil marks.
Find two cells with exactly the same two candidates. The cells must share both a box and a row or column.
If both cells contain only {2, 7}, one must be 2 and the other 7. Remove 2 and 7 from every other cell in their shared line and their shared box.
A Locked Pair is a Naked Pair that works in two regions. Pointing Pair instead tracks two positions of a single digit.
Find three cells in the intersection of a line and a box. Their combined candidates must contain exactly three different digits.
For example, {2, 7}, {2, 9} and {7, 9} reserve 2, 7 and 9 for those three cells. Remove all three digits from the rest of both the line and the box.
Each cell can contain two or three of the digits. Count the combined candidates; this is a Naked Triple shared by two regions.
Inside one box, a digit has exactly two possible cells, and both are in the same row or column.
The box must place the digit in one of those two cells. That supplies the digit to their shared line, so remove it from the line outside the box.
Check the whole box for other positions. Pair means two cells for one digit, not two different digits.
Inside one box, a digit has exactly three possible cells, all in the same row or column.
Whichever of those three cells takes the digit, the shared line already has it. Remove the digit from that line outside the box.
Verify that no other cell in the box contains the digit. Triple counts three positions of the same digit.
In a row or column, a digit has exactly two possible cells, both in the same box.
The line must place the digit in one of these two cells. The box therefore gets its copy there too; remove the digit from the box outside the line.
Start by checking the entire line. This is the line-to-box direction of Locked Candidates.
In a row or column, a digit has exactly three possible cells, all in the same box.
The line needs one copy of the digit and all its options are in this box. Remove the digit from every cell of the box outside that line.
Three candidates in a box alone are not enough: they must be all remaining positions in the starting line.
Connect an even number of at least four cells that all have the same two candidates. Consecutive cells must see each other.
Along a chain of {2, 7} cells, values alternate 2, 7, 2, 7, or 7, 2, 7, 2. The endpoints therefore contain different digits. A cell that sees both endpoints can contain neither 2 nor 7.
Use an even number of cells and keep exactly the same pair throughout. Only remove candidates from cells that see both endpoints.
Find two nonseeing cells with the same pair {a, b} in two different boxes of one band or stack. In the third box, inspect the line not occupied by either endpoint. It allows a but no b.

If both endpoints were b, they would block b in two lines of the third box. Its remaining line has no b either, which is impossible. At least one endpoint is a, so remove a from every cell that sees both endpoints.
A band is three boxes across; a stack is three boxes down. Single refers to one removable digit, not necessarily one affected cell.
Use two nonseeing {a, b} cells in two boxes of the same band or stack. In the third box, the line not occupied by either endpoint allows neither a nor b.
The endpoints cannot both be a: the third box would have nowhere for a. They cannot both be b for the same reason. They must be different, so cells seeing both endpoints lose both digits.
Check both digits in the third box, including filled cells. If only one digit is absent, use the single form instead.
Start with the double form of Chute Remote Pair: two nonseeing {a, b} endpoints and neither digit available in the unused line of the third box.

Both digits must appear in the other two lines of the third box. Together with the two endpoints, they occupy those lines. In each endpoint box, remove a and b from other cells on either of those two lines, as well as from common peers of the endpoints.
Bonus means extra eliminations beyond the common peers. Follow the two lines through all three boxes; exchange rows and columns for a stack.

Choose two cells in a line–box intersection whose combined candidates are four digits. Find a bivalue cell in the line outside the box and another in the box outside the line. Their pairs must be disjoint and together equal those four digits.

The two intersection cells see both wings. The wings cannot repeat a digit because their candidate pairs are disjoint. All four cells therefore take four different digits. The line wing pair is locked to the line; the box wing pair is locked to the box. Remove each pair from the rest of its region.
For example, wings {1, 2} and {3, 4} support intersection cells using only 1, 2, 3 and 4. This lesson teaches the Type 1 form used by the hint.

Choose three cells in a line–box intersection whose combined candidates are five digits. Use a bivalue wing in the line and another in the box, both outside the intersection. Their pairs must be disjoint and contained in those five digits.

The five pattern cells must take different digits. Each wing pair is locked to its own region. The fifth digit is only in the intersection, so it is locked to both regions. Remove the line pair from the line, the box pair from the box, and the extra digit from both, outside the pattern.
Compared with Type 1, there is one extra intersection cell and one extra digit. Verify both wings and the full five-digit union before eliminating.
For one digit, connect conjugate pairs: exactly two possible positions in a region. Color each connected pair with opposite colors, continuing through one connected component.
One color is true throughout the component and the other false. An uncolored candidate that sees both colors conflicts with a true candidate in either case, so it can be removed.
This is color trap. Seeing just one color proves nothing. Do not combine colors from separate components.
Build one alternating-color component using conjugate pairs for a single digit. Look for two candidates of the same color in one row, column or box.
All candidates of one color share a truth value. The conflicting same-color candidates cannot both be true, so that entire color is false and the opposite color is true.
This is color wrap. The contradiction must be inside one connected component; matching colors in unrelated components do not form a proof.
Build a single-digit chain with alternating strong and weak links, starting and ending strong. If its distinct endpoints see each other, their weak link closes a continuous loop.
Follow the loop in either direction. Each weak link is forced to have one true endpoint. Remove the digit from outside cells that see both ends of any weak link in the loop.
Include the closing link. This continuous loop differs from the one-endpoint form, which proves a placement.
Build a single-digit chain whose strong and weak links alternate. Return to the starting candidate on a strong link, so that the meeting candidate has a strong link on each side.
Assume the meeting candidate is false. Alternating inferences take you around the chain and force that same candidate true. The assumption contradicts itself, so place the digit in the meeting cell.
The conclusion is a placement at the meeting candidate. Check the alternating links and the two strong links at that meeting point.
Build an XY-Chain through bivalue cells. Its endpoints contain the same elimination digit and also see each other, closing the chain.
As in an open XY-Chain, if the shared digit is false at one endpoint, it is true at the other. An outside cell that sees both endpoints cannot contain that digit.
Every chain cell must have exactly two candidates. Follow the outgoing digit of each cell into the next, and exclude the chain cells from the targets.
Use a rectangle in two rows, two columns and exactly two boxes. Three corners have only {a, b}; the fourth has extra candidates and just one of a or b.

The fourth corner cannot take its remaining rectangle digit: that would create the ambiguous a/b rectangle that a unique-solution puzzle must avoid. Remove that remaining rectangle digit from the fourth corner.
The m marks a missing rectangle candidate. The other three corners must still be the exact same pair, and this reasoning requires a unique solution.

Two corners on one side are exactly {a, b}. On the other side, one corner contains both plus extras, and one contains only a plus extras. In a region shared by these latter two cells, a is confined to them.
If the full corner were b, the conjugate link would force the incomplete corner to a, leaving the forbidden two-digit rectangle. Remove b from the full corner.
This is the missing-candidate form of Type 4. Check the conjugate link, both pure corners, the two-box rectangle and uniqueness.
In a two-box rectangle, one corner is exactly {a, b}. Each of the other three contains exactly {a, b, z}, with the same extra digit z.

If all three extra z candidates were false, every corner would reduce to {a, b}, creating the forbidden interchangeable rectangle. At least one of those three corners is z. Remove z from cells seeing all three.
Type 5+ has three possible extra-digit corners. Seeing only two of them is insufficient; the puzzle must have a unique solution.
Two diagonal corners of a two-box rectangle are exactly {a, b}; the other diagonal contains both digits plus extras. One digit, a, is confined to the rectangle in its two rows and two columns.

The a positions form an X-Wing. If a occupied the two corners with extras, the pure corners would be b, giving the interchangeable a/b rectangle. Uniqueness rules this out: keep a in the pure corners, removing b there and a from the other two corners.
Verify the row and column restrictions for a, not just the rectangle shape. This numbered variant uses the same uniqueness assumption as the other UR lessons.
Start with a two-box rectangle containing a pure {a, b} corner. At its diagonally opposite corner, a forms conjugate links along both the row and the column to the adjacent rectangle corners.

If the opposite corner were b, those two conjugate links would make both adjacent corners a. The pure corner would then be b, producing the forbidden interchangeable rectangle. Remove b from the opposite corner.
Both links for a are required. Check the whole row and column, as well as the pure corner and unique-solution assumption.
Assume one candidate is true and follow its consequences. Some deductions may need two or more earlier facts together; retain every required premise.
If this assumption forces an invalid state, it is false. For example, a cell losing all candidates or a digit losing all positions in a region disproves the starting candidate. Remove that candidate.
A net joins facts within the same assumption. A branching drawing alone is not enough: the joined facts must actually be needed to continue.
Take one candidate and consider both possibilities: true and false. Follow a chain from each assumption.

If both cases force the same candidate true, place it. If both force it false, remove it. The starting candidate must be either true or false, so the shared conclusion holds. If an assumption instead leads to a contradiction, its opposite truth value is proved directly.
Compare the same candidate and the same truth value in both branches. Keep the branches separate until comparing their conclusions.
Consider a candidate true and false in separate branches. Within each branch, deductions may combine multiple earlier facts.

A placement or elimination reached in both branches is unconditional. A joined deduction is valid only when all its premises follow within that same branch. If one starting assumption leads to a contradiction, the opposite truth value is proved directly.
Never combine a fact from the true branch with one from the false branch. They are alternatives, not simultaneous facts.
Choose an unsolved cell. Start one branch for each of its remaining candidates, assuming that candidate fills the cell.
Exactly one branch describes the solution. If every branch forces the same candidate true or every branch forces it false, apply that shared placement or elimination.
Include every candidate of the starting cell. Finding agreement in only two branches of a three-candidate cell is insufficient.
Start a separate branch for every candidate of one cell. Inside a branch, use multiple earlier facts together when a deduction requires them.
If all branches agree on a placement or elimination, it follows regardless of the cell value. Each combined deduction must use facts from its own branch only.
Cover all starting candidates. Two branches agreeing does not make a net by itself; a net needs a deduction that depends jointly on several facts.
Choose one digit in a row, column or box. Start a branch for every remaining position of that digit in the region.
The digit must occupy one of these positions. If all branches force the same placement or elimination, that conclusion must hold.
This is also called Unit Forcing Chain. Include every possible position in the starting region, not just a convenient pair.
Choose a digit and a region. Branch from each possible position of that digit. Inside a branch, allow deductions that require several preceding facts together.
A conclusion shared by every starting position is valid. The joined premises for any deduction must belong to the same branch.
Region and Unit mean a row, column or box. Check both complete coverage of starting positions and the premises at every join.
For one digit, find 5 rows whose remaining positions all lie in the same 5 columns. The roles of rows and columns can also be exchanged.
Each of the 5 base rows needs the digit, and no two copies can share a column. The 5 cover columns are therefore occupied by these rows. Remove the digit from those columns outside the base rows.
Check every candidate in the base rows, including positions at incomplete crossings. In a standard 9×9 grid, a complementary smaller fish may be easier to find.
For one digit, find 6 rows whose remaining positions all lie in the same 6 columns. The roles of rows and columns can also be exchanged.
Each of the 6 base rows needs the digit, and no two copies can share a column. The 6 cover columns are therefore occupied by these rows. Remove the digit from those columns outside the base rows.
Check every candidate in the base rows, including positions at incomplete crossings. In a standard 9×9 grid, a complementary smaller fish may be easier to find.
For one digit, find 7 rows whose remaining positions all lie in the same 7 columns. The roles of rows and columns can also be exchanged.
Each of the 7 base rows needs the digit, and no two copies can share a column. The 7 cover columns are therefore occupied by these rows. Remove the digit from those columns outside the base rows.
Check every candidate in the base rows, including positions at incomplete crossings. In a standard 9×9 grid, a complementary smaller fish may be easier to find.
Use exactly 8 cells with 8 distinct candidates in total. Divide them into a pivot group and two wing groups. Each wing and the pivot together share a region. The wings share exactly one digit, z.

If z is absent from the pivot, at least one wing must contain z, so a target seeing both entire wings cannot be z. If the pivot also allows z, the required z may be in any of the three groups; a target must see the entire pattern. In either case, placing z in the target would leave too few distinct values for the pattern.
Count cells and distinct digits separately, and verify all cross-group visibility. This is the Sudoku Coach 8-Y-Wing definition, not a general ALS-XZ label.
Use exactly 9 cells with 9 distinct candidates in total. Divide them into a pivot group and two wing groups. Each wing and the pivot together share a region. The wings share exactly one digit, z.

If z is absent from the pivot, at least one wing must contain z, so a target seeing both entire wings cannot be z. If the pivot also allows z, the required z may be in any of the three groups; a target must see the entire pattern. In either case, placing z in the target would leave too few distinct values for the pattern.
Count cells and distinct digits separately, and verify all cross-group visibility. This is the Sudoku Coach 9-Y-Wing definition, not a general ALS-XZ label.
